prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "ELI LILLY & Co" (ticker LLY). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Eli Lilly shows several Rule Breaker traits: it is the top dog in the fast-growing obesity drug market (about 60% of US incretin prescriptions), the shares rose about 40% over the past year versus about 20% for the S&P 500, and the stock is often called expensive. It is an unusual Rule Breaker, though, as a 150-year-old pharma company rather than a young disruptor.
summaries.buffett: Lilly fits several Buffett tenets: an understandable franchise in tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound), high returns on capital (ROIC about 42%) and rising earnings. But drug moats expire with patents, US price pressure is growing, and at about 39 times trailing earnings the price leaves little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger was willing to pay up for exceptional businesses, and Lilly's R&D engine and obesity lead come close to that description. Inverting the problem, the main failure paths are faster-than-expected price cuts, new obesity competitors and heavy dependence on one molecule (Mounjaro and Zepbound were about 56% of 2025 revenue).
summaries.lynch: Lynch would call Lilly a fast grower in a stalwart's body: revenue rose 45% in 2025 to $65.2B and EPS nearly doubled to $22.95. At a P/E of about 39 and a PEG ratio of about 1.4 it is not a bargain by his rule, and it is heavily covered by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: Lilly scores strongly on Fisher's points: management keeps developing new products (orforglipron, retatrutide, Kisunla), R&D clearly produces results, margins are high (83% gross, about 40% operating in 2025) and the company sells effectively, including through LillyDirect. Weaker points are rising debt and dependence on government pricing decisions.
summaries.graham: Lilly fails most of Graham's price tests: about 86 times average 2023-2025 earnings and a P/E times P/B above 1,000, and it reported a net loss of $204M in 2017 because of US tax reform. It passes on size, on dividends paid every year since 1885 and on EPS growth from $2.26 in 2015 to $22.95 in 2025.
summaries.thiel: Lilly answers several of Thiel's questions well: tirzepatide is clearly better than the previous best drug (20.2% vs 13.7% weight loss against semaglutide in SURMOUNT-5), the timing for obesity treatment is right, and it has strong distribution. It falls short of a durable monopoly because patents expire and Novo Nordisk and many new entrants are competing.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a sensible price; Lilly offers some of the strongest growth among mega-caps (2026 revenue guidance of $85-87B, up about 32%) but an FCF yield of only about 1.75%. Its valuation depends on obesity sales staying strong despite price cuts.
summaries.druckenmiller: Lilly fits Druckenmiller's earnings-driven approach: earnings are accelerating, guidance was raised in August 2026, and the stock has outperformed the market over the past year. Drug-pricing policy and new competitor launches are the key risks he would watch.
summaries.smith: Lilly matches much of Terry Smith's model: very high gross margins (about 83%), high returns on capital and a large runway in obesity and diabetes, and Fundsmith has owned pharma stocks of this kind. The price, at about 39 times trailing earnings, is the main point of tension with 'don't overpay'.
summaries.greenblatt: On a Magic Formula screen Lilly scores well on return on capital (ROIC about 42%) but poorly on earnings yield, with EV/EBIT of about 27 (an earnings yield near 3.7%). It would likely rank in the middle rather than near the top.
summaries.akre: Lilly fits Akre's three-legged stool fairly well: an exceptional business in tirzepatide, capable long-serving management under David Ricks, and large reinvestment opportunities in new plants and the pipeline. The price is high, and insiders own only about 0.2% directly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks low-risk bets bought cheaply; Lilly is a high-quality business but trades at about 39 times trailing earnings and 31 times book, far from a bargain. It would fit his framework only after a large price fall.
summaries.wood: Lilly fits part of Cathie Wood's framework through its push into new drug platforms (oral GLP-1s, gene editing) that relate to multiomic medicine, but it is not a core ARK-style platform innovator. Its growth is driven mainly by conventional drug development rather than falling technology costs.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, cash-generative businesses with moats; Lilly's obesity franchise is dominant and fast-growing, but heavy capex and $54.9B of debt against $9.0B of cash (June 2026) and pricing risk make it less predictable than his typical holding. It is a quality business priced at a premium.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model partly fits: Lilly has cut cash prices of obesity drugs to the $199-$299 per month range and expanded LillyDirect, using scale to widen access. Whether this strengthens its moat or just reflects price pressure remains to be seen.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for big markets with painful problems, and obesity and diabetes affect hundreds of millions of people, which Lilly addresses with leading products. As a 150-year-old company worth about $1 trillion, it lacks the early-stage upside he sought.

momentum.evidence: LLY rose about 40% over the 52 weeks to October 13, 2026 (to $1,166.51), versus about a 20.4% total return for the S&P 500 (SPY).

g4.evidence: CEO David Ricks has led Lilly since 2017 through the tirzepatide boom, and the Lilly Endowment is a major long-term shareholder.

g6.evidence: Some commentators call Lilly expensive at about 39 times trailing earnings and 31 times book, while many analysts see it as reasonably priced for its growth.

simple.evidence: Lilly's main business (selling patented medicines such as Mounjaro and Zepbound) is easy to understand, but judging clinical trials, patents and drug pricing needs specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $24.5B in 2020 to $65.2B in 2025, and operating income rose from $6.1B to $26.3B.

integrity.evidence: Management has a strong delivery record and capped insulin costs at $35 a month in 2023, but insiders own only about 0.2% and the company still faces criticism over US drug prices.

b6.evidence: Lilly has focused on its own R&D in incretins, oncology, immunology and neuroscience, with targeted acquisitions rather than large empire-building mergers.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 42% (trailing), but debt rose to $54.9B by June 2026 against $9.0B of cash, so returns are partly debt-funded.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $9.0B in 2025, only about 43% of $20.6B of net income, because of heavy plant spending; trailing FCF of $18.2B is about 68% of net income.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded tirzepatide and new plants, and Lilly's market value grew to about $1.04 trillion, far more than the earnings it kept.

safety.evidence: At about 39 times trailing earnings and 31 times book, the price is not below a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 30 and a PEG of about 1.4 are high but not extreme given 2026 revenue guidance of about 32% growth.

mu5.evidence: Lilly has a diverse pipeline, but heavy dependence on tirzepatide, government price cuts and new obesity rivals are real risks.

reinvest.evidence: Lilly is reinvesting heavily in new plants and a deep pipeline (orforglipron, retatrutide), with ROIC of about 42% showing high returns on that capital.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower: revenue rose 45% in 2025 and guidance implies about 32% growth in 2026.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 39 is below 2025 EPS growth (from $11.71 to $22.95), but the PEG ratio on forward estimates is about 1.4.

runway.evidence: Hundreds of millions of people live with obesity or diabetes, and tirzepatide is expanding into sleep apnea, heart failure and other uses, with consensus FY2028 revenue near $107B.

ly7.evidence: There is no notable insider buying, but the share count fell about 0.6% over the past year.

ly8.evidence: Lilly is one of the most widely followed stocks, with about 28 analysts covering it and a market value near $1 trillion.

fi2.evidence: Lilly launched Foundayo (orforglipron), Kisunla, Ebglyss and Jaypirca and plans to file retatrutide in early 2027 as older drugs like Trulicity mature.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced tirzepatide, which beat semaglutide in the SURMOUNT-5 trial (20.2% vs 13.7% weight loss), and the first oral small-molecule GLP-1.

fi4.evidence: Lilly held about 60% of US incretin prescriptions and built a direct-to-patient channel, LillyDirect.

longterm.evidence: Lilly built tens of billions of dollars of manufacturing capacity ahead of approvals and keeps raising R&D spending.

gr1.evidence: Lilly had $65.2B of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $1.04 trillion in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: Lilly reported a net loss of $204.1M in 2017 because of charges related to US tax reform.

gr4.evidence: Lilly has paid a dividend every year since 1885, and its current annual dividend is $6.92 per share.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $2.26 in 2015 to $22.95 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: Average 2023-2025 EPS ($5.80, $11.71, $22.95) is about $13.49, so the $1,166.51 price is about 86 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 39 times a P/B of about 31 gives over 1,200, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Tirzepatide is clearly better than semaglutide (20.2% vs 13.7% weight loss), but that is a large gain rather than ten times better.

timing.evidence: Obesity is now treated as a chronic disease, cash-pay and Medicare access are expanding, and the incretin market was estimated at about $79B in 2025.

th3.evidence: Lilly started in diabetes and grew into the much larger obesity market, but it entered as a challenger to Novo Nordisk rather than with a big share of a small market.

team.evidence: David Ricks's team made early, bold bets on tirzepatide and manufacturing that turned Lilly into the world's most valuable drug company.

th5.evidence: Lilly has a large sales force, payer relationships and its own LillyDirect channel selling Zepbound vials directly to patients.

durable.evidence: Its pipeline and scale support a lasting position, but tirzepatide's patents expire in the 2030s and generic GLP-1s are spreading.

th7.evidence: Lilly saw early that dual GIP/GLP-1 drugs could lead obesity treatment, but Novo Nordisk and many others now pursue the same market.

trend.evidence: Lilly is the leading beneficiary of the shift to treating obesity with incretin drugs, a major secular trend in health care.

dr1.evidence: Trailing EPS rose to $29.79 from $22.95 in 2025, and in August 2026 Lilly raised 2026 revenue guidance to $85.0-$87.0B.

dr2.evidence: Foundayo's oral launch and retatrutide data could improve results by 2028, beyond current tirzepatide sales.

dr4.evidence: Drug demand is largely independent of the economy, but US government pricing policy is a headwind.

dr6.evidence: Identifiable catalysts include the planned retatrutide filing in early 2027, Foundayo uptake and new tirzepatide indications.

dr7.evidence: Lilly's growth and lead support high conviction, but concentration in one molecule and pricing risk argue against an outsized position.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of $18.2B gives an FCF yield of about 1.75%, low for its growth given heavy capex.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 27.4, an operating earnings yield of about 3.7% on enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: Lilly is growing fast with record results rather than in a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: The business is strong and diverse, but at about 39 times earnings a pricing or competitive shock could cause a large share-price loss.

wo1.evidence: Lilly is investing in gene editing and genetic medicines, which relate to multiomic sequencing, but its leadership comes from conventional drug development.

wo2.evidence: Scale has let Lilly cut cash prices for obesity drugs to the $199-$299 per month range, opening wider demand, but this is driven by policy as well as cost.

wo3.evidence: Lilly's growth comes mainly from one area, incretin drugs, rather than several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: The obesity market could grow several times over as oral drugs spread, but not likely many times larger than today in five years.

ac3.evidence: Drug demand is insulated from commodities and rates, but US drug-pricing policy and tariffs are major outside forces.

ns1.evidence: Lilly lowered cash prices for Zepbound and capped insulin costs, but these moves were also prompted by government pressure.

ns4.evidence: Its pipeline should keep it strong, but patent expiries and many new obesity rivals make a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: Obesity and diabetes affect hundreds of millions of people and drive heart disease and other illnesses, and tirzepatide cuts body weight by about a fifth on average.
